topic.title: How McDonald's really makes money: it's a landlord

title: Every burger you buy pays McDonald's rent 🍔
description:
If it isn't the burgers, how does McDonald's really make its money?
An animated story with illustrative numbers; the characters are not advisers.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.
cta: Did you know you were paying rent? Comment

lines.text: It's not the burgers. So how does McDonald's really make money?
Picture one restaurant selling $4,000,000 of food a year. Three clues explain where that money goes, and the last one is under your feet.
Clue one: the owner. Most of these restaurants are run by a local franchise owner, who pays for the kitchen, the staff and the food.
Clue two: every sale. Spend $20 on a meal, and say 15% of it goes to McDonald's as rent and fees. That's $3 off every tray.
Is that all? The burgers must make them way more than $3.
Clue three: the land. McDonald's often owns or leases the ground under the restaurant, so the owner pays it rent every month.
Every tray adds up. In a year, this one corner sends McDonald's about $600,000, whether the burgers make a profit or not.
That's the twist I love. The owner carries the risk on every burger, but McDonald's collects the rent either way, like a landlord.
So McDonald's earns like a landlord, and the burgers pay the rent. Over 20 years, one corner hands it about $12.0M.
So every burger I buy pays someone's rent? Then what is McDonald's really selling, if...
